analysis.investment_thesis: L.K. Mehta Polymers fails both Magic Formula screens catastrophically: a P/E of 26.9 implies an earnings yield near 3.7% (vs. my 12%+ threshold), while ROE of 0.08% signals near-zero return on capital. This is neither cheap nor good — the opposite of what the Magic Formula seeks.
key_strengths: High promoter holding at 72.92% signals skin in the game
Debt-light micro-cap trader, balance sheet likely simple
Dual exposure to plastics and gold trading offers some diversification
key_risks: ROE of 0.08% indicates capital is earning essentially nothing
Earnings yield ~3.7% is deeply overvalued vs. risk-free rate
Pure trading business (plastics + gold) has no moat and razor-thin margins
red_flags: ROE 0.08% — effectively zero return on capital
P/E 26.9 on a negligible-profit trading micro-cap is irrational
17.5 Cr market cap with negligible FII interest (0.21%) — liquidity and governance risk
Mixing plastic ropes/granules and gold trading suggests unfocused capital allocation
analysis.detailed_analysis:
From a Magic Formula lens, this is a textbook reject. Earnings yield (EBIT/EV) cannot exceed the inverse of P/E (1/26.9 ≈ 3.7%), and after adjusting for cash/debt it's unlikely to clear even 5% — far below the 12% minimum I demand. ROE of 0.08% is a proxy for ROIC here since this is a trading outfit with little fixed-asset leverage, and it tells me invested capital earns roughly nothing. You cannot have a "good business at a bargain price" when the business isn't good and the price isn't a bargain.

Trading businesses in commodity plastics and gold inherently lack the pricing power that drives high returns on capital — they're pass-through spreads on working capital. At 17.5 Cr market cap with 72.9% promoter holding, this is a thinly-traded shell-like micro-cap where reported earnings can be whipsawed by a single inventory mark. The systematic answer is unambiguous: skip this and let the screener surface something that ranks well on both factors.
